Revised question

What exactly does the proposed Mann–Whitney AUROC measure, and how can it be checked without threshold sampling?

The source adds pairwise AUROC for two groups. Its exact formula is a finite combinatorial count. It is invariant under strictly increasing score transformations, while group balancing and causal intervention are separate questions.

Definitions and assumptions

Let positive scores p₁,…,p_m and negative scores n₁,…,n_k be real. Assume both sample sizes are nonzero. Count a strict win as one and a tie as one half.

Define U=Σ_(i,j)[1_(p_i>n_j)+1/2·1_(p_i=n_j)] and AUROC=U/(mk).

Exact pairwise interpretation

AUROC is the probability that a uniformly chosen positive has larger score than an independently uniformly chosen negative, with ties split equally. It is unchanged by any strictly increasing transformation of all scores.

Derivation or proof

There are exactly mk equiprobable positive-negative pairs; summing their declared win values and dividing gives the probability statement. A strictly increasing function preserves strict inequalities and equalities, so every pair contribution remains unchanged. The half-tie convention ensures that if every score is equal, AUROC is exactly 1/2. A decreasing transformation reverses wins and losses and changes the value to 1−AUROC. None of these rank identities controls calibration, prevalence-specific precision or intervention effects.

Worked example

Use positive scores (2,3) and negative scores (1,2).

The four pair contributions are 1,1/2,1,1, summing to 7/2. Thus AUROC=7/8=0.875. Applying exp to every score leaves 7/8; negating every score gives 1/8.

The requested statistic can be certified by exact finite counting rather than a numerical ROC grid.

Revised question

Reconstruction: How many signed-edge configurations survive vertex gauge transformations, and which spectral statistic detects a cycle flux?

The source reports a finite gauge/parton preflight and explicitly limits its physical interpretation. We construct a graph theorem that can actually be proved: the gauge quotient is a binary cycle space, and even a three-cycle has a flux-dependent adjacency spectrum.

Definitions and assumptions

On a connected finite graph with v vertices and e edges, assign s_e∈{±1}. A vertex gauge g_v∈{±1} changes s_{uv} to g_us_{uv}g_v.

The flux around a cycle is the product of its edge signs. A signed adjacency matrix has entries s_{uv} on edges and zero otherwise; gauge change is conjugation by diag(g).

Z₂ gauge classes are counted by cycle rank and retain a flux detectable in the spectrum

There are 2^{e−v+1} gauge classes, classified by the signs on the e−v+1 non-tree edges after fixing every edge of a spanning tree to +1. Flux and adjacency spectrum are gauge invariant.

Derivation or proof

Choose a root and spanning tree. Set its gauge to +1 and propagate the remaining vertex gauges so that each tree edge becomes positive. This is possible uniquely once the root gauge is chosen, because a tree has a unique path to every vertex. A simultaneous sign flip of every gauge acts trivially, so the effective gauge group has 2^{v−1} elements and acts freely on edge assignments of a connected graph. The residual non-tree signs are independent, giving 2^{e−v+1} orbits. Each is the product around the corresponding fundamental cycle, because every tree sign is now positive. Every other cycle flux is a product of fundamental-cycle fluxes. Matrix conjugation preserves eigenvalues, and each gauge factor in a cycle product appears twice, proving both invariances.

Worked example

Use the triangle graph with all three edge signs initially positive, then flip one edge.

The all-positive adjacency has characteristic polynomial t³−3t−2=(t−2)(t+1)². Flux −1 gives t³−3t+2=(t+2)(t−1)². Their spectra are (2,−1,−1) and (−2,1,1). Both configurations have the same absolute edge weights and unsigned graph, but their flux and signed spectra differ. There are exactly two gauge classes because e−v+1=1.

This is an exact finite reason a flux-aware proxy can distinguish cases that a hopping-magnitude-only proxy misses.

Scope

The theorem is combinatorial. It does not prove a quantum phase, a numerical gap claimed by a parton approximation, or a thermodynamic-limit distinction.

Further development

For a specified larger graph, compute its complete flux coordinates and compare signed Laplacian spectral gaps within each gauge class, retaining finite-size and physical-approximation boundaries.

Revised question

Reconstruction: Which constraint makes two bosonic modes a finite-dimensional spin representation?

The May source names Schwinger bosons and slave-fermion partons without providing a complete operator construction. The two-boson realization below is exact algebra: a number constraint selects one spin representation. It does not treat an unconstrained enlarged Hilbert space as the original spin system.

Definitions and assumptions

Let a,b satisfy [a,a†]=[b,b†]=1 and all cross commutators zero on the algebraic Fock space. Define J₊=a†b, J₋=b†a, J_z=(N_a−N_b)/2 and N=N_a+N_b.

For an integer n≥0, the N=n sector has orthonormal basis |r,n−r⟩, r=0,…,n.

Schwinger bosons realize the spin algebra on each fixed-particle sector

[J_z,J₊]=J₊, [J_z,J₋]=−J₋ and [J₊,J₋]=2J_z. The N=n sector is invariant, has dimension n+1 and Casimir J_z²+(J₊J₋+J₋J₊)/2=(n/2)(n/2+1)I.

Derivation or proof

Use the canonical commutators to obtain [N_a,a†]=a† and [N_b,b]=−b. These prove the first two identities, and all J operators commute with N because every raising in one mode lowers the other. Next J₊J₋=N_a(N_b+1) and J₋J₊=N_b(N_a+1); their difference is N_a−N_b. Their symmetric average is N_aN_b+N/2. Adding J_z²=(N_a²−2N_aN_b+N_b²)/4 gives N²/4+N/2. On N=n this is the stated scalar. The ladder action J₊|r,n−r⟩=√((r+1)(n−r))|r+1,n−r−1⟩ connects every basis vector, so there is no proper invariant ladder subspace; this is spin j=n/2. The proof uses only finite particle sectors, avoiding unbounded-operator domain claims.

Worked example

Take n=2, corresponding to spin one.

The J_z eigenvalues are −1,0,1. J₊ connects the first to the second and the second to the third with coefficient √2; it annihilates the top state. The Casimir is 2I. For n=1 the dimension is two and the Casimir is 3I/4. These matrices can be verified symbolically by storing squared ladder coefficients.

The construction has a precise constraint, matrix representation and complete algebraic certificate.

Scope

The bosonic Fock space without N=n is a direct sum of many spins. A mean-field parton ansatz requires projection and an independent argument for observables; this algebra alone does not validate it.

Further development

Derive a specified spin Hamiltonian in the constrained bosonic representation and compare exact small-system spectra before introducing any mean-field decoupling or thermodynamic-limit interpretation.

Revised question

Reconstruction: Which theorem can replace a finite-size observation valley claim with a precise recovery condition?

The retrieved OGL statistics describe finite dimensions and a later weakening of a proposed Haar lemma. They do not supply all observation channels. We formulate a newly stipulated linear observation model whose recovery and blindness statements are exact, and leave the historical composite statistics empirical.

Definitions and assumptions

Let A:R^n→R^m be linear, with observed data y=Ax+e and ||e||≤ε. For a subspace V of admissible displacements define σ_V=inf{||Av||:v∈V,||v||=1}.

Recovery is considered modulo an identified symmetry subspace K⊂kerA; choose V=K⊥. A positive σ_V is a restricted coercivity constant.

Observation geometry has exact invisible subspaces and a noise-to-state bound

Two admissible states x,z with x−z∈V and both residuals at most ε satisfy ||x−z||≤2ε/σ_V when σ_V>0. Exact recovery modulo K holds if and only if kerA=K. If σ_V=0 in finite dimension, a nonzero invisible displacement remains.

Derivation or proof

The triangle inequality gives ||A(x−z)||≤||Ax−y||+||Az−y||≤2ε. The definition of σ_V then proves the bound. In finite dimension the unit sphere in V is compact, so the infimum is attained. It is positive exactly when A has no nonzero kernel vector in V. Because K⊂kerA and every vector decomposes orthogonally into K and V, this is equivalent to kerA=K. If there is a unit v in kerA∩V, then every x+tv has the same data for all real t, so no finite uniform state-error bound can hold. Thus a valley in a numerical score is not itself a recovery theorem: the crucial mathematical object is the least restricted singular value, with its declared admissible subspace and normalization.

Worked example

Take A(x₁,x₂,x₃)=(x₁,x₂) and K=span(e₃).

On V=span(e₁,e₂), σ_V=1, so the identified coordinates differ by at most 2ε. Full-state recovery is impossible because x₃ is invisible. Adding a third channel δx₃ with δ>0 yields singular values 1,1,δ and full-state error at most 2ε/min(1,δ). At δ=1/100, noise can be amplified by a factor one hundred in the weakest direction.

The model gives a constructive geometry of recovery, symmetry blindness and conditioning.

Scope

The historical T0/T1/HARD classifications and the quoted Haar mean are not verified from this model. A random-matrix concentration theorem needs the actual distribution and Lipschitz statistic.

Further development

Revised question

Reconstruction: Which observer statistic is a mathematical identity, and why can a logarithm of mutual information fail metric axioms?

The recovered OGL formulas include mutual and conditional mutual information, a modular Hamiltonian and a proposed logarithmic distance. We separate exact finite facts from geometric interpretation. In particular, two-site support cannot establish emergent locality in a system containing only two sites.

Definitions and assumptions

Use entropy in bits, S(ρ)=−trρlog₂ρ, and I(A:B)=S_A+S_B−S_AB. For a strictly positive two-qubit density matrix, K=−logρ has an expansion in the sixteen Pauli strings.

Every nonidentity Pauli string on two qubits has support one or two. Define OCI as the squared norm of those components divided by the squared norm of all nonidentity components, when that denominator is nonzero.

Derivation or proof

The May discussion contrasted classical existence, constructibility and choice. A concrete finite-ring theorem gives positive witness-producing mathematics. It also prevents an unwarranted conclusion that every classical existence proof must already carry an efficient algorithm.

Definitions and assumptions

A finite commutative ring R has an explicitly enumerable underlying set and computable addition and multiplication tables. An ideal is a subset containing zero, closed under addition and multiplication by all ring elements.

A maximal proper ideal is a proper ideal contained in no strictly larger proper ideal. A finite search is constructive when it returns a witness with a terminating verification.

A finite maximal-ideal algorithm separates constructive witnesses from unrestricted choice

Every finite nonzero commutative unital ring has a maximal proper ideal, and exhaustive search returns one. For Z/12Z the maximal ideals are (2) and (3), giving quotient fields F₂ and F₃.

Derivation or proof

Enumerate all subsets of R and test the finite closure conditions for an ideal. At least the zero ideal is proper because 1≠0. Among the finitely many proper ideals choose one of maximal cardinality; no strictly larger proper ideal can exist, so it is maximal. Termination follows from the finite subset count 2^{|R|}. If I is maximal and x∉I, the ideal generated by I and x must be R. Thus 1=i+rx for some i∈I,r∈R, and [r][x]=1 in R/I. Every nonzero quotient element is invertible, proving the quotient is a field. In Z/12Z, ideals correspond to divisors d of 12, and maximality occurs when the quotient Z/dZ is a field, namely d=2 or 3. This is a completely finite witness procedure, although its exponential cost makes it unsuitable as a general efficiency claim.

Worked example

Enumerate ideals of Z/12Z through their divisor generators.

The proper ideals are (0),(2),(3),(4),(6); (2) contains six residues and (3) four. The quotient sizes are two and three, and their nonzero residue classes have inverses. The ideal (6) is not maximal because it lies properly inside (2).

The example provides both an existence proof and an explicit checkable witness.

Scope

For arbitrary infinite rings, the usual maximal-ideal theorem is proved with a choice principle such as Zorn’s lemma. That fact neither makes finite algebra nonconstructive nor makes every consequence of ZFC algorithmically decidable.

Definitions and assumptions

On ℓ²(N₀), let A have diagonal eigenvalues n, n≥0. The heat operator H_t=e^{−tA} has eigenvalues e^{−tn}, t>0.

A positive diagonal operator is trace class exactly when its diagonal entries have a finite sum. Small-time heat behavior concerns t→0 rather than a fixed t.

A heat-trace asymptotic is different from a trace-class statement at a fixed time

H_t is trace class for every t>0, with TrH_t=1/(1−e^{−t})=t^{−1}+1/2+O(t) as t→0. Its trace diverges as t→0, and H_t converges strongly to the noncompact identity. The trace-norm truncation tail after n=N is e^{−t(N+1)}/(1−e^{−t}).

Derivation or proof

The geometric series gives the trace and exact tail, all terms being nonnegative. Taylor expansion 1−e^{−t}=t−t²/2+O(t³) and division give the small-time expansion. For a fixed vector x∈ℓ², ||(H_t−I)x||²=Σ_n|e^{−tn}−1|²|x_n|² tends to zero by dominated convergence, since the multiplier is bounded by one. Identity is not compact because the standard basis has no norm-convergent subsequence. Thus trace-class operators can converge strongly to a noncompact operator while their trace norms diverge. This does not contradict trace-norm closedness because convergence is only strong. For a trace difference, a cancellation of leading asymptotic coefficients likewise says nothing by itself about whether the corresponding operator difference is trace class at a fixed parameter.

At t=log2 the heat eigenvalues are 2^{−n}.

The full trace is two. Keeping indices n=0,…,9 gives trace 2−2^{−9}, and the exact positive tail is 2^{−9}=1/512. At t=log2/2 the trace is 1/(1−1/√2)=2+√2, showing sensitivity to the time scale without any failure of trace class.

A separate approved-grounded set G⊆S changes admissibility to R⊆G and may require evidential repair even when asserted support already contains R. For the graph limitation, take three Boolean constraints x=0, y=0 and x∨y=1. Every pair has a satisfying assignment, so the compatibility graph is a triangle and its full vertex set is a maximal clique. All three together are inconsistent. Thus pairwise compatibility is insufficient for arbitrary logic unless an additional theorem proves a Helly-type or pairwise-to-global property for the chosen constraint family.

Reconstruction: What composition rule prevents a derived certificate from silently exceeding the authority of its premises?

The May artifact calculus proposed a six-coordinate authority profile. A precise finite poset model makes the intended monotonicity rule executable, while retaining the distinction between an order-theoretic accounting theorem and the truth of any mathematical assertion entered into the system.

Definitions and assumptions

Let A={0,1,2}⁶ with coordinatewise order and meet a∧b given by coordinatewise minimum. A dependency graph is a finite directed acyclic graph; every node has a local authority cap c(v).

For a source node set a(v)=c(v). At any later node define a(v)=c(v)∧∧_{u→v}a(u). The coordinates are abstract bookkeeping levels, not measured probabilities.

Authority composition is a meet calculation with an explicit proof dependency graph

For every node v, a(v) is the meet of c(w) over all ancestors w of v, including v. It is the largest profile simultaneously bounded by all those caps. Adding an additional dependency can only decrease or preserve the profile.

Derivation or proof

Order the graph topologically. The claim is immediate for a source. If it holds for the predecessors of v, substituting their ancestor meets into the defining equation gives exactly the union of their ancestor sets together with v; repeated factors do not matter because meet is idempotent. This proves the formula by induction. Any other profile bounded by every ancestor cap is bounded by their meet, so the formula is the greatest admissible profile. Enlarging the ancestor set introduces further meet factors and cannot raise any coordinate. None of these steps supplies a proof that an individual premise is true: that requires a separately checked derivation. A soundness statement is conditional: if the local inference rules preserve truth and the source propositions are true, induction through the same graph proves every output proposition true.

Worked example

Use two premises with profiles a=(2,2,1,2,1,2) and b=(2,1,2,2,2,1), and a local cap c=(2,2,2,1,2,2).

The output meet is (2,1,1,1,1,1). A later node whose only extra cap is (1,2,2,2,2,2) receives (1,1,1,1,1,1). Swapping premise order or duplicating a premise changes neither result. A forgotten dependency with first coordinate zero would reduce that coordinate to zero, exposing why the dependency set itself must be complete.

The calculus now has a small genuine theorem: maximal admissible authority propagates by a meet, with a transparent dependency invariant.

The numerical labels are newly stipulated ordinal levels. A profile is not a theorem prover, an uncertainty probability, or evidence that a reported software suite ran.

Its differential vanishes because da=0 and the derivation identity gives d[a,a]=[da,a]−[a,da]=0. Thus it defines a cohomology class, not merely a vector norm. In the displayed algebra take every bracket involving b or c to be zero; all Jacobi identities then vanish because the only nonzero bracket lands in central c. The derivation identity also holds, including d[a,b]=0 and its right side−[a,c]=0. For α=t a−t²b, dα=−t²c and [α,α]/2=t²c, cancelling at every order. If instead db=0, c is a nonzero cohomology class and no coefficient can cancel it.

With d=0 the same [a,a]/2=c is nonzero in H², so even an arbitrarily small nonzero t cannot solve the formal equation beginning with a. The obstruction criterion is exact and its solvable and obstructed cases are explicit.

A cubic over a field is reducible if and only if it has a linear factor. Here f(0)=f(1)=1, proving irreducibility and hence that the quotient is a field. Its nonzero multiplicative group has seven elements; α is neither zero nor one, and Lagrange implies its order is seven because seven is prime. Direct reduction with α³=α+1 also verifies α⁷=1. In any field of characteristic two, squaring respects sums and products, so Frobenius is a homomorphism. It is injective and hence surjective on a finite field. Every nonzero element has seventh power one, so x⁸=x for every element; thus the third iterate is identity. Applying Frobenius to f(α)=0 proves the conjugate equations. The three conjugates are distinct because α has order seven and the exponents1,2,4 differ modulo seven. An embedding is therefore a concrete substitution map, not merely an equality of field sizes.

Use binary representations to enumerate α powers.

They are1,α,α²,α+1,α²+α,α²+α+1,α²+1,then1. None of the first seven nonzero powers repeats. The map α↦α² is an automorphism; the map α↦1 is not a field homomorphism from this presentation because f(1)=1≠0. A primitive-root test must actually exclude the identity element, especially when the group order is prime.

The example provides a full arithmetic table and explicit automorphism certificate.

Definitions and assumptions

For a species a₁≥a₂≥⋯≥0 of finite support set d_j=a_j−a_{j+1}≥0. Let P_j=∏_{i≤j}p_i and w_j=logP_j.

Define S(t)=#{d of finite support:Σ_jd_jw_j≤t}. For s>0 set Z(s)=∏_{j≥1}(1−e^{−sw_j})^{−1} and F(s)=logZ(s).

The least representative satisfies m(a)=∏P_j^{d_j}; thus species with least representative at most N are exactly the partitions counted by S(logN). The Euler product converges for every s>0, and S(t)≤exp(F(s)+st).

Derivation or proof

Because a_i=Σ_{j≥i}d_j, rearranging the finite sums gives logm=Σ_i a_i logp_i=Σ_jd_jΣ_{i≤j}logp_i. This proves the product identity and the bijection, since differences recover d uniquely. Also w_j≥jlog2, so Σ_je^{−sw_j} converges geometrically. For all sufficiently large j the terms are at most1/2, and −log(1−x)≤2x there; hence F(s) converges. Expanding each nonnegative geometric series gives Z(s)=Σ_dexp(−sΣd_jw_j), justified by monotone convergence. Every partition of weight at most t contributes at least e^{−st}; therefore S(t)e^{−st}≤Z(s), proving the bound. For a finite t only weights w_j≤t can occur, so S(t) can also be computed by a finite exact recursion using integer primorial products, avoiding logarithmic rounding.

The representatives are1,2,4,6,8,12, giving six species: empty,(1),(2),(1,1),(3),(2,1). Here P₁=2,P₂=6,P₃=30>12, so only d₁,d₂ can be nonzero. The inequality2^{d₁}6^{d₂}≤12 yields four cases at d₂=0 and two at d₂=1. This is an exact integer enumeration.

Revised question

Reconstruction: Which hypotheses actually prove the leading constant in the species count, without claiming an unproved local saddle prefactor?

The May source proposes a specific logarithmic asymptotic. We give its leading-scale derivation conditional on explicitly stated Laplace asymptotics obtainable from the prime number theorem. The proof does not certify the more delicate finite-saddle prefactor.

Definitions and assumptions

Use the weighted species partition function F(s) from the preceding entry and t=logN. Assume as s↓0 that F(s)~C/[slog(1/s)], −F′(s)~C/[s²log(1/s)] and F″(s)~2C/[s³log(1/s)], with C=π²/6.

Under the tilted law, the independent d_j are geometric with P_s(d_j=r)=(1−e^{−sw_j})e^{−srw_j}. Their total weight W has mean −F′(s) and variance F″(s).

The species exponential scale follows from a tilted-measure argument under explicit prime asymptotics

Under these hypotheses, logS(t)~2√(2Ct/logt), hence logS(logN)~(2π/√3)√(logN/loglogN). The assumptions follow from the counting asymptotic #{j:w_j≤x}~x/logx plus standard positive-kernel Laplace estimates; those estimates are identified as an analytic input here.

Derivation or proof

The Euler-product upper bound is F(s)+st. Choose s asymptotic to √(2C/[tlogt]); then log(1/s)~(1/2)logt and each term F(s),st is asymptotic to √(2Ct/logt), proving the limsup. For the lower bound fix ε∈(0,1/2) and choose s so that E_sW=(1−ε)t. Such a value exists for large t by continuity and the assumed mean asymptotic. Then Var_sW/t² is asymptotic to 2(1−ε)/(st), which tends to zero. Chebyshev implies P_s((1−2ε)t≤W≤t)→1. Since S(t)=e^{F(s)}E_s[e^{sW}1_{W≤t}], it is at least e^{F(s)+s(1−2ε)t} times that probability. Taking logarithms, dividing by √(2Ct/logt), and using the corresponding s asymptotic gives a lower coefficient tending to two as ε↓0. Together with the upper bound this proves the leading constant. It deliberately uses a broad concentration window rather than an unproved density approximation at one exact weight.

Worked example

Check the saddle scale algebraically with C=π²/6.

The stationary balance is t≈C/[s²log(1/s)]. Replacing log(1/s) by(1/2)logt yields s≈π/√(3tlogt), so2st≈(2π/√3)√(t/logt). The tilted relative variance is O(√(logt/t)), which vanishes and makes the broad-window lower bound possible.

The proposed leading constant has a precise conditional theorem and a proof mechanism.

Scope

The verifier checks the finite partition model and symbolic scale constants; it does not prove the prime number theorem or a local central limit theorem. No finite-N accuracy or prefactor is inferred.

Further development

Prove the three Laplace estimates directly from primorial-weight counting with effective remainders, then develop a quantitative local limit theorem to justify the source’s finite-saddle correction.

Revised question

Reconstruction: Why does descending exponent order on ascending primes minimize the represented integer?

The SIT fragment specifies species (3,2,1), least representative360 and arithmetic invariants. We formulate the underlying optimization exactly and prove its general rearrangement rule. This is independent of whether the historical Lean tranche compiled.

Definitions and assumptions

A species is a finite nonincreasing list a₁≥⋯≥a_r≥1 of prime exponents. Its representatives are positive integers with that multiset of nonzero exponents. Let p_i denote the i-th prime.

Define the least candidate m(a)=∏_{i=1}^r p_i^{a_i}. Arithmetic invariants are Ω=Σa_i, ω=r and τ=∏(a_i+1).

An exponent species has a unique least integer representative

m(a) is the unique least positive integer in its species. Its divisor-count, total-prime-factor and distinct-prime-factor invariants are exactly the stated product and sums.

Derivation or proof

First any chosen r distinct primes q₁<⋯<q_r satisfy q_i≥p_i. Replacing them by the first r primes without changing exponent assignments cannot increase the product and strictly decreases it if any chosen prime differs. Next if p<q but exponents a<b are assigned in the wrong order, compare p^a q^b with p^b q^a: their ratio is (q/p)^{b−a}>1. Swapping the exponents strictly decreases the number. Repeated exchanges put the exponents in descending order on ascending primes. Equality permits only swaps among equal exponents, which do not change the integer, proving uniqueness of the numerical minimizer. Every divisor independently chooses an exponent between zero and a_i, yielding τ; counting factors with and without multiplicity gives Ω and ω.

Worked example

Take a=(3,2,1).

The least integer is2³·3²·5=360. Its τ is4·3·2=24, Ω=6 and ω=3. Swapping the first two unequal exponents gives2²·3³·5=540, larger by3/2. Using primes2,3,7 instead gives504, larger by7/5. Exhaustively assigning these exponents to the first few primes verifies the exchange proof’s finite predictions.

The least-representative theorem gives SIT a concrete arithmetic object and an exact comparison principle.

Scope

The species forgets prime labels and therefore does not determine additive behavior, residue classes or an elliptic invariant. A theorem entry in a manifest is not a compiled formal proof.

Further development

Develop exact algorithms that enumerate least representatives below N using monotone exponent bounds, and prove completeness through the exchange rule and a recursive prime-power cutoff.

Revised question

Reconstruction: Which lattice and generating-polynomial invariants are determined solely by an exponent species?

The source gives D(360) as C₄×C₃×C₂ and links rank coefficients to τ and lattice height to Ω. These statements admit a direct complete proof, with a useful rank symmetry that goes beyond merely counting divisors.

Definitions and assumptions

If n=∏p_i^{a_i}, order its positive divisors by divisibility. Represent d=∏p_i^{b_i} by the vector (b_i), 0≤b_i≤a_i. Give it rank ρ(d)=Σb_i.

Let R_n(t)=Σ_{d|n}t^{ρ(d)} and Ω(n)=Σa_i. A chain C_{a_i+1} is the totally ordered set {0,…,a_i}.

The divisor lattice is a product of chains with a symmetric rank polynomial

D(n)≅∏C_{a_i+1} as lattices, with meet and join given by coordinate minima and maxima. R_n(t)=∏(1+t+⋯+t^{a_i}); R_n(1)=τ(n), its degree is Ω(n), and t^{Ω(n)}R_n(t^{−1})=R_n(t).

Derivation or proof

Unique factorization makes the divisor-vector correspondence bijective. Divisibility is coordinatewise inequality, so greatest lower and least upper bounds are coordinatewise minimum and maximum, proving the lattice isomorphism. Multiplying the finite geometric polynomials records every independent choice of b_i once, proving the rank formula. Substitution t=1 counts all choices and hence all divisors. The top vector has rank Σa_i, and every saturated chain from bottom to top increments one exponent at a time, giving that height in edges. The involution d↦n/d replaces each b_i by a_i−b_i and reverses rank, proving coefficient symmetry and the reciprocal polynomial identity. Thus not only τ and Ω, but the full rank distribution, is determined by the species.

Worked example

For n=360 use exponents3,2,1.

R(t)=(1+t+t²+t³)(1+t+t²)(1+t)=1+3t+5t²+6t³+5t⁴+3t⁵+t⁶. The coefficients sum to24, and the longest chain has six edges. Complementary ranks zero/six, one/five and two/four have matching counts. The rank-three divisors are the six choices of exponent sum three inside the box.

The product-of-chains description yields exact combinatorics and a canonical duality.

Scope

Lattice isomorphism forgets actual prime values. Different integers of the same species have the same divisor lattice but can differ radically in size and arithmetic congruences.

Further development

Construct a symmetric chain decomposition of this product lattice and derive unimodality of the rank coefficients; formalize the decomposition as a finite combinatorial witness rather than relying on a plotted histogram.

Revised question

Reconstruction: What can be proved from a baseline coercivity margin and a sum of perturbation debits, and what is a separate local-to-global obstruction?

The geological structured-object passage combines generators, admissible cones, coercivity and cohomological gluing. We preserve two mathematically precise components instead of asserting that an analogy supplies a universal geological spectral theory. Both models below are newly stipulated.

Definitions and assumptions

Let A act on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space with Re⟨x,Ax⟩≤−α₀||x||². Let perturbations E_i satisfy ||E_i||≤δ_i. Define α_eff=α₀−Σδ_i.

For local scalar data on a triangle, assign oriented edge differences a₁₂,a₂₃,a₃₁ with a_ji=−a_ij. A global potential means a_ij=u_j−u_i for some vertex values.

A coercivity debit ledger and a finite gluing obstruction have independent exact meanings

The perturbed generator A+ΣE_i has coercivity margin at least α_eff, and a positive α_eff proves exponential norm decay. The triangle data glue to a potential exactly when a₁₂+a₂₃+a₃₁=0; this obstruction is unrelated to the sign of α_eff unless an additional model couples them.

Derivation or proof

For the analytic statement, Re⟨x,E_ix⟩≤||E_i||||x||²≤δ_i||x||². Summing gives the new quadratic-form bound, and differentiating the squared norm along the flow proves decay as in the Lyapunov argument. The bound is sharp: scalar perturbations E_i=δ_iI applied to A=−α₀I attain equality. For gluing, summing potential differences around the cycle telescopes to zero, proving necessity. If the sum is zero, choose u₁=0,u₂=a₁₂,u₃=a₁₂+a₂₃; then the third difference is exactly a₃₁, proving sufficiency. Adding the same constant to all potentials is the only ambiguity. This constructive solution exhibits an actual cohomological compatibility condition in a finite setting. A small analytic perturbation norm neither forces that condition nor follows from it.

Worked example

Take α₀=1, δ₁=1/5 and δ₂=3/10, and edge data(2,3,−5).

The effective margin is1/2, so the norm decays at least as e^{−t/2}. The local edge data glue to potentials(0,2,5). Replacing the final edge by−4 gives obstruction one and makes gluing impossible, while leaving the analytic margin unchanged. Conversely increasing a debit past the baseline destroys the positive decay certificate even if the edge sum remains zero.

The source’s ledger and gluing language now refer to separate exact theorems with explicit inputs.

Scope

No mineral reaction kinetics, geological parameter values, empirical spectra or field-scale holonomy is certified. An admissible cone additionally requires an invariance proof, not only a coercivity inequality.

Further development

For a measured reaction network, supply a stoichiometric conservation matrix, a positively invariant concentration cone and a weighted Lyapunov metric, then analyze gluing of local parameter estimates separately from dynamical stability.

Definitions and assumptions

Breath-stream capture arithmetic is a transparent volume-to-mass balance

The flow of carbon-dioxide volume isQx, measured in m³/hour. Multiplying by density gives kg/hour, multiplying by recoveryη gives the captured rate and integrating over hours gives kilograms. The ppm conversion is essential:3000ppm is0.003, not0.3. For varying inputs the integral follows by summing small time intervals and taking the Riemann limit under ordinary bounded regularity. The product-of-averages issue is already visible with two time intervals: if high flow always coincides with low concentration, the covariance is negative and EQx<EQ Ex. A concentration average must be flow-weighted to preserve the total mass, namely x_weighted=∫Qx/∫Q when the denominator is positive. Efficiency and density variations require their own weighting as well.

Reconstruction: When is P_X+P_Z−P_XP_Z valid, and what can be asserted without independence?

The source gives a two-sector failure product and fitted threshold candidates. We replace an implicit independence assumption with an exact joint-probability formula, then add a finite confidence calculation. Threshold fitting is kept distinct from a theorem about arbitrarily large devices.

Definitions and assumptions

Let X and Z be failure events with probabilities p_X, p_Z and intersection r. Their combined failure is the union. Feasibility requires max(0, p_X+p_Z−1)≤r≤min(p_X, p_Z).

If n independent identically distributed trials each have failure probability p, the probability of zero observed failures is(1−p)^n. Independence of trials is separate from independence of sectors within one trial.

Two-sector failure has a correlation parameter and a rigorous confidence envelope

P(X∪Z)=p_X+p_Z−r, hence max(p_X, p_Z)≤P(X∪Z)≤min(1, p_X+p_Z). The product formula1−(1−p_X)(1−p_Z) holds exactly when r=p_Xp_Z. After zero failures in n trials, the one-sided level1−δ upper confidence bound is p≤1−δ^{1/n}.

Derivation or proof

The union identity follows by partitioning into the three disjoint regions X\Z, Z\X and X∩Z. The intersection bounds follow from nonnegative probabilities of all four cells; conversely those bounds make the four cell probabilities r, p_X−r, p_Z−r,1−p_X−p_Z+r nonnegative and summing to one, so the bounds are sharp. Sector independence is exactly the additional equality r=p_Xp_Z. For the zero-failure bound, a candidate p above1−δ^{1/n} makes the zero-count event have probability belowδ. Inverting this binomial test gives the stated confidence procedure; it is a coverage statement about repeated sampling, not a posterior probability that the fixed parameter lies in the interval.

Worked example

Take p_X=p_Z=1/10 and n=100 independent trials with zero observed combined failures.

Independent sectors give combined failure19/100. Perfectly coincident sectors give1/10, and disjoint sectors give1/5. At δ=1/20 the zero-failure confidence upper bound is1−(1/20)^{1/100}≈0.029513. A point estimate zero is therefore not a proof of zero failure probability.

The reported sector model can now state exactly where correlations and finite evidence enter.

Revised question

Reconstruction: When do two deterministic state updates commute, and why is a footprint graph only a sufficient model?

The late-June runtime source gives conflict graphs from mutation and admission footprints. We formulate a finite state theorem that explains the legitimate mathematical role of those sets. It does not infer successful execution or freshness from a diagram alone.

Definitions and assumptions

A state is a functionσ:V→D on finitely many variables. An actionAreads onlyR_A⊆Vandchanges onlyW_A⊆V: its changed values depend solely onσ restricted toR_A.

Two actions satisfy the symmetric noninterference conditionsW_A∩(R_B∪W_B)=∅andW_B∩(R_A∪W_A)=∅. An admission condition may additionally require selected variables to retain specified values.

Read-write footprint independence gives a sufficient commutation certificate

Under these conditions, A∘B=B∘Aon every state. A plan of pairwise noninterfering actions can be reordered arbitrarily without changing the final state. The conditions are sufficient rather than necessary.

Derivation or proof

Because Bdoes not write any variable inR_A, action A sees the same read values before and after B; similarly B sees unchanged read values through A. Their write sets are disjoint, so neither overwrites the other’s outputs. On W_A each order therefore gives the same A value, on W_B the same B value, and outside the union the original value remains. This proves commutation coordinatewise. Any permutation is a product of adjacent swaps, so pairwise commutation proves arbitrary reordering by induction on swaps. Necessity fails, for example, when two actions both set the same variable to the same constant: their write sets overlap but their maps commute. Conversely disjoint write sets alone are insufficient because one may read a value the other changes.

Let Aset x:=y+1andBset z:=2w, with variablesx, y, z, wdistinct.

The write sets{x}and{z}are disjoint from both other read sets, so the actions commute. If Binsteadsets y:=0, thenAafter Bgives x=1, while B after A retainsx=y_old+1; they need not commute. A receipt basedonyis invalidated by that write unless its admission condition explicitly tolerates the change.

The conflict graph has a proved noninterference meaning and a sharp counterexample to a weaker rule.

Scope

Revised question

Which exact polynomial and boundary witnesses suffice to certify the seven-point spectrum?

The July1 source reports a rational spectral-rigidity theorem with support0,1,2,4,5,6,8. Its original matrix and boundary seeds are not fully retrieved. A complete general certificate states exactly what those missing data would need to establish, and gives an explicit rational model rather than adopting an unseen computation.

Definitions and assumptions

Let S={0,1,2,4,5,6,8} and p(t)=∏_{λ∈S}(t−λ). Let T be an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional rational vector space. Define e_λ(t)=∏_{ν∈S,ν≠λ}(t−ν)/(λ−ν).

Lagrange spectral certificate

If p(T)=0, then E_λ=e_λ(T) are pairwise disjoint idempotents, sum to I and satisfy T=ΣλE_λ. The spectrum equals S exactly when every E_λ is nonzero; one vector with E_λv≠0 certifies each nonzero projector.

Derivation or proof

On the seven roots, e_λ(ν)=δ_λν. Thus e_λ²−e_λ, e_λe_ν for λ≠ν, Σe_λ−1 and t−Σλe_λ all vanish on S and are divisible by the square-free polynomial p. Evaluating at T proves the identities. The image of E_λ consists of λ-eigenvectors because(t−λ)e_λ is divisible by p. Their direct sum is the entire space, so p(T)=0 also proves semisimplicity rather than merely listing possible eigenvalues. Conversely a nonzero E_λ supplies an eigenvector, making the support criterion exact. A spectral list alone would not exclude a Jordan block, for which p(T) could fail. The same projectors compute every polynomial observable: h(T)=Σh(λ)E_λ. For z outsideS they also give the exact resolvent(zI−T)^{-1}=ΣE_λ/(z−λ), verified by multiplication. Thus the certificate supplies inversion and spectral decomposition, not just an eigenvalue list. Its denominators are explicit rational differences between distinct roots.

Worked example

Take T=diag(0,1,2,4,5,6,8) and v=(1,1,1,1,1,1,1).

Each E_λv is the corresponding standard basis vector. All seven eigenvalues therefore occur. The minimal polynomial is p, and seven independent boundary projections certify the full support without numerical diagonalization.

An exact rational certificate is a polynomial identity plus explicit support witnesses, with no floating eigenvalue tolerance.

Scope

This does not reproduce the reported Theorem C until its actual T and seed vectors are supplied. An arbitrary matrix sharing the spectrum need not share other structure.

Revised question

What quotient is defined by the two quadrics, and what changes when all cubic monomials are added?

The July3 target specifies two quadrics and a Hilbert function(1,2,1,0). The quadrics alone do not have that finite Hilbert function. An invertible coordinate change makes both the obstruction and the intended cubic closure completely explicit over every field.

Definitions and assumptions

Let k be any field and λ∈k. In k[a,b] set Q=(a²−λ²b²,ab−λb²). Let m=(a,b),u=a−λb and v=b. The coordinate change is invertible with a=u+λv.

Exact jet normal form

Q=(u²,uv). Its quotient has Hilbert function1,2,1,1,1,… and is not Artinian. Adding m³ gives I=(u²,uv,v³), with basis1,u,v,v² and Hilbert function(1,2,1,0,…).

Derivation or proof

The second quadric becomes uv. The first becomes u²+2λuv, so subtracting2λ times the second gives u²; this works even in characteristic two. Conversely these formulas recover the original generators. Every quotient monomial is then a power of v or the single monomial u; powers v^d survive in every degree. Adding all cubics kills v³, while u³,u²v,uv² were already killed. The four remaining monomials are independent because the ideal is monomial and none is divisible by u²,uv or v³. Thus the desired finite jet depends essentially on the cubic-closure hypothesis, not on a two-prime experimental agreement. The finite quotient has maximal ideal generated byu,v, with square spanned byv² and cube zero. Its socle containsu andv² and has dimension two. Consequently its symmetric Hilbert function does not make it a Gorenstein algebra: the multiplication pairing from degree one to the top degree is degenerate becauseu annihilates both generators.

Worked example

Use λ=2 over Q or over F₇.

With u=a−2b,v=b, the original quadrics are u²+4uv and uv. Both fields give the same four standard monomials after cubic closure. Without closure, v⁴ survives, contradicting the claimed terminal zero Hilbert coefficient.

The coordinate calculation gives a characteristic-independent constructive model and states precisely which quotient is being studied.

No larger W₁ containment or stage-N computation is inferred from this local normal form. Its relation to those packets needs an actual map and ideal certificate.

Definitions and assumptions

Let R=k[x,y],A=R/(x²,xy,y³). Its socle is{x∈A:(x,y)x=0}. Use φ=[[y,0],[−x,y²],[0,−x]], whose columns are syzygies among the ordered generators x²,xy,y³.

Exact minimal graded resolution

There is a minimal resolution0→R(−3)⊕R(−4)→R(−2)²⊕R(−3)→R→A→0. A has basis1,x,y,y² and socle span{x,y²}, so its type is two.

Derivation or proof

The two column relations are yx²−x(xy)=0 and y²(xy)−x(y³)=0. To prove they generate every syzygy, let ax²+bxy+cy³=0. Setting x=0 implies x divides c; write c=xc₁. Divide by x to get ax+by+c₁y³=0. Setting y=0 implies y divides a; write a=ya₁. Then b=−xa₁−y²c₁. This is a₁ times the first column plus−c₁ times the second. Injectivity of φ follows from ya₁=0 and−xc₂=0 in the domain R. All entries lie in the homogeneous maximal ideal, proving minimality. Multiplication by x,y on the four standard monomials gives the stated socle. The alternating graded resolution gives Hilbert numerator1−2t²−t³+t³+t⁴=1−2t²+t⁴. Dividing by(1−t)² yields1+2t+t². The cancellation of the two degree-three terms in this numerical series conceals their distinct homological origins, which is why the Hilbert series alone cannot decide whether the displayed resolution is a complete intersection.

Compare with B=R/(x²,y²).

Both A and B have Hilbert function(1,2,1). But B has socle span{xy} and total Betti numbers(1,2,1), whereas A has a degree-one socle class x and type two. The Hilbert numerator of A has a cancellation at degree three that does not cancel a minimal free module.

Which finite-field conclusions lift to Q, and what certificate proves an exponent or ideal containment?

Definitions and assumptions

Let p,q be distinct primes and M an integer matrix. A polynomial membership witness for f∈(g₁,…,g_s) over Q is an exact identity Df=Σh_ig_i with D a nonzero integer and h_i integral polynomials. Minimal nilpotence exponent also requires a valid nonmembership witness for the preceding power.

One-sided rank lifting and a two-prime counterexample

Which sign makes two commuting differentials into a total differential, and why does the mapping cone test chain-map compatibility?

The retrieved July discussion includes double complexes, Koszul signs and mapping cones. These operations become rigorous only after fixing degrees and signs. A small rational example exposes the failure that an unsigned sum would conceal.

Definitions and assumptions

Let C^{p,q} have horizontal δ:C^{p,q}→C^{p+1,q} and vertical ∂:C^{p,q}→C^{p,q+1}, with δ²=∂²=0 and δ∂=∂δ. Total degree is p+q. For a cochain map f:C→D, Cone(f)^n=D^n⊕C^{n+1}.

Signed totalization and cone criterion

D_tot=δ+(−1)^p∂ satisfies D_tot²=0. The cone differential d(d,c)=(d_Dd+fc,−d_Cc) squares to zero precisely when f commutes with the differentials.

On bidegree(p,q), the mixed term from δ followed by the signed vertical map has sign(−1)^{p+1}, whereas the reverse mixed term has sign(−1)^p. They cancel because δ and ∂ commute; their pure squares vanish. In the cone, applying d twice gives first component d_D²d+(d_Df−fd_C)c and second component d_C²c. Thus the only possible obstruction is exactly the chain-map defect. The shift and its minus sign are indispensable. A cone records whether f is a quasi-isomorphism: its long exact cohomology sequence follows by taking the short exact sequence D→Cone(f)→C[1] and tracing cocycle representatives. In particular Cone(id) is contractible; an explicit homotopy is h(d,c)=(0,d), since dh+hd=(d,c). The characteristic matters to the diagnostic example: in characteristic two the unsigned product2 vanishes, so that particular numerical failure disappears. The sign convention nevertheless remains the correct degree bookkeeping over arbitrary rings and is necessary for uniform compatibility with shifts, tensor products and cone triangles. A rational example avoids concealing the issue behind2=0.

Tensor two complexes Q --id→ Q in degrees0 and1.

The total groups have dimensions1,2,1. With degree-one coordinates ordered(horizontal,vertical), d⁰(1)=(1,1) and d¹(a,b)=−a+b. Their product is zero, and ker d¹=span(1,1)=im d⁰, so the total complex is acyclic. Using the unsigned map a+b instead gives d¹d⁰(1)=2, which fails over Q.

All tensor products are algebraic over a field k. Hom denotes all linear maps. A duality datum for V consists of a vector space W, evaluation ev:W⊗V→k and coevaluation coev:k→V⊗W satisfying the two triangle identities.

Adjunction and the finite-dimensional duality criterion

Derivation or proof

Given F:V⊗W→U, send v to the map w↦F(v⊗w). Conversely a linear map v↦G_v gives the bilinear pairing(v,w)↦G_v(w), which factors uniquely through V⊗W. The constructions are inverse by evaluation on pure tensors; naturality follows by composition. For finite-dimensional V with basis e_i and dual basis e^i, take W=V*, ev(φ⊗v)=φ(v) and coev(1)=Σe_i⊗e^i. Either triangle identity reduces to v=Σe^i(v)e_i. Conversely every algebraic tensor coev(1) is a finite sum Σ_{i=1}^r v_i⊗w_i. The triangle identity then writes every v as Σv_i ev(w_i⊗v), so V is spanned by finitely many v_i. This proves necessity and explains why a formal infinite basis sum is not an algebraic tensor. Naturality can also be checked explicitly: replacingv byw(v) before currying is the same as precomposing the resulting mapV→Hom(W,U), and postcomposingF byU→U′ commutes with pointwise postcomposition. Thus the isomorphism respects the actual morphisms, which is the additional content of an adjunction beyond equality of two dimensions.

Take V=Q², W=Q³, U=Q and F(v⊗w)=vᵀMw with M=[[1,2,3],[4,5,6]].

Which rational numbers have finite duodecimal expansions, and how are periodic expansions certified?

Definitions and assumptions

Use digits0,…,9,A,B for values0,…,11. For a rational0≤a/b<1 in lowest terms, long division sets r₀=a,12r_j=b d_{j+1}+r_{j+1}, with0≤r_{j+1}<b. A bar denotes infinite repetition.

Termination and periodicity criterion

The base-twelve expansion of a/b terminates exactly when b divides12^N for some N, equivalently b has no prime factors except2 and3. Every rational has an eventually periodic expansion; after removing the2- and3-parts of the denominator, the period divides the multiplicative order of12 modulo its remaining part.

Derivation or proof

AfterN steps the division identities telescope to a/b=Σ_{j=1}^N d_j12^{-j}+r_N/(b12^N). Termination is equivalent to r_N=0 and hence to b|12^N because gcd(a,b)=1. Conversely that divisibility forces zero remainder. Only finitely many remainders occur, so a nonzero remainder must eventually repeat and the deterministic update then repeats forever. When the denominator is coprime to12, the remainder is12^j a modb and the first return occurs at the multiplicative order of12. Powers of2 and3 contribute only a finite preperiod. An expansion ending in infinitely manyB digits is the familiar alternate representation of a terminating number; choosing the non-B-tail convention restores uniqueness. The same remainder identity certifies truncation error without a decimal approximation: afterN digits the omitted fraction is exactlyr_N/(b12^N), betweenzero and12^{-N}. For a repeating block oflengthh, multiplying by12^h and subtracting yields a rational denominator12^h−1. These two identities provide exact conversion in both directions.

Represent2026,1/8 and1/5 in base twelve.

2026=1·12³+2·12²+0·12+10, so it is120A₁₂. Also.16₁₂=1/12+6/144=1/8. For1/5 the remainders follow1→2→4→3→1 and the digits are2,4,9,7. Thus1/5=.overline{2497}₁₂; equivalently(2·12³+4·12²+9·12+7)/(12⁴−1)=4147/20735=1/5.

Each symbolic statement reduces to an integer identity and a finite remainder certificate.

Revised question

When does increasing approximation resolution remain compatible with vanishing data noise, uniformly over a specified model class?

The recovered master inequality becomes useful only after the model class, data norm and quantifiers are fixed. The fundamental issue is that approximation can improve while noise amplification becomes arbitrarily large. A diagonal parameter choice reconciles these two limits without requiring a guessed convergence rate.

Definitions and assumptions

Let A:X→Y be bounded between normed spaces, let M⊂X be a specified nonempty class, and let R_n:Y→X be bounded linear maps. Data satisfy yδ=Ax+e with ||e||≤δ.

Define B_M(n)=sup_{x∈M}||R_nAx−x||, S(n)=||R_n||, and Eδ(R_n;M)=sup_{x∈M,||e||≤δ}||R_n(Ax+e)−x||. Assume B_M(n) is finite and tends to zero.

Uniform bias–noise decomposition and diagonal regularization

Eδ(R_n;M)≤B_M(n)+δS(n). There exists an integer choice n(δ)→∞ with Eδ(R_{n(δ)};M)→0. Every choice with B_M(n(δ))→0 and δS(n(δ))→0 has this property.

Derivation or proof

Add and subtract R_nAx and apply the triangle inequality and the operator norm bound. For existence choose a strictly increasing sequence n_j with B_M(n_j)≤1/j. Put s_j=max(1,S(n_1),…,S(n_j)), and choose strictly decreasing positive d_j→0 with d_j≤1/(j s_j). For d_{j+1}<δ≤d_j use n(δ)=n_j. Then δS(n(δ))≤1/j and the total bound is at most 2/j. As δ→0 the interval index j→∞, hence the result. This proof does not assume that S is monotone or that B has a power-law rate. Uniform convergence of B is a substantive hypothesis: pointwise convergence R_nAx→x for each fixed x does not imply it on an arbitrary unbounded class. If A has a nonzero kernel and M contains x and x+h with h∈ker A, a uniform error tending to zero is impossible, since the data coincide. Thus the model class must encode identifiable information as well as approximation smoothness.

Worked example

Use a diagonal inverse problem on ℓ², Av=(v_k/k), the cutoff R_N and the ellipsoid M={x:Σk²|x_k|²≤1}.

The tail is bounded by 1/(N+1), while S(N)=N. With N=⌊δ^(−1/2)⌋ and 0<δ≤1/4, the error is at most 1/(N+1)+δN≤2√δ. At δ=1/100, N=10 gives the sharper explicit bound 1/11+1/10=21/110.

The same resolution parameter has a measurable cost and a justified accuracy bound. Unregularized inversion has unbounded norm and no such deterministic noise guarantee.

Scope

The bound is deterministic and uniform over M. It does not estimate unknown noise, identify M from data, or imply that the two upper-bound terms can always be simultaneously attained.

Further development

Construct a parameter rule from a known noise bound and a verifiable model hierarchy M_j, then prove an oracle inequality showing how far the selected resolution can be from the best admissible one.

Revised question

Can the polynomial cutoff rate be proved with both an upper bound and a matching impossibility argument?

The source rate δ^{r/(p+r)} has a clean deterministic interpretation. It is the minimax order for a diagonal operator with polynomial singular values and a Sobolev-type ellipsoid. A two-point indistinguishability argument supplies the lower bound, so the rate expresses an information limitation rather than only the quality of one algorithm.

Definitions and assumptions

Take X=Y=ℓ², Ae_k=k^(−p)e_k with p>0, and M_r={x:Σk^{2r}|x_k|²≤1}, r>0. Let R_N invert the first N coordinates and discard the rest.

The deterministic minimax error is inf over all maps T:Y→X of sup_{x∈M_r,||e||≤δ}||T(Ax+e)−x||. The map T need not be linear or continuous.

Matching polynomial upper and lower rates

For sufficiently small δ>0, spectral cutoff with N=⌊δ^(−1/(p+r))⌋ has worst-case error O(δ^{r/(p+r)}). No reconstruction map improves this order uniformly on M_r under norm-bounded noise.

Derivation or proof

For x∈M_r, Σ_{k>N}|x_k|²≤(N+1)^(−2r)Σ_{k>N}k^{2r}|x_k|², so B(N)≤(N+1)^(−r). Also ||R_N||=N^p, because its diagonal coefficients are k^p. The master bound is therefore (N+1)^(−r)+δN^p. The stated N balances the two terms and gives the upper order. For the lower bound put K=⌈δ^(−1/(p+r))⌉ and v=K^(−r)e_K. Both v and −v belong to M_r and ||Av||=K^(−(p+r))≤δ. The observation zero can thus arise from v with noise −Av or from −v with noise Av. For any output z=T(0), the triangle inequality gives max(||z−v||,||z+v||)≥||v||. Since K≤2δ^(−1/(p+r)) for δ≤1, this is at least 2^(−r)δ^{r/(p+r)}. This applies to every possible estimator. It also explains why stronger algorithms alone cannot remove the smoothness–noise tradeoff.

Worked example

Set p=r=1 and δ=10^(−4).

N=100 gives error at most 1/101+1/100<0.02. K=100 gives two opposite feasible signals ±e_100/100 that both produce zero within the noise budget. Every estimator has worst-case error at least 0.01.

Cutoff is optimal up to a factor below two in this example; the exponent is exact at the level of uniform deterministic rates.

Scope

This is a diagonal ellipsoid model. Replacing its coefficient condition by the pointwise assertion |x_k|≤Ck^(−s) changes the tail exponent to s−1/2 when s>1/2. The two smoothness conventions must not be silently identified.

Further development

Extend the two-point proof to singular values comparable, rather than equal, to k^(−p), retaining explicit comparison constants and determining when adaptation to unknown r costs a logarithmic factor.

Revised question

Which cutoff actually proves the logarithmic convergence rate when singular values decay exponentially?

A bare rule N≈(log(1/δ)/c)^{1/β} can conceal a failure: at the exact leading balance, amplified noise can remain of order one. Subtracting a log-log term yields a valid convergent rule while preserving the advertised logarithmic rate. The lower bound again follows from two indistinguishable signals.

Definitions and assumptions

Let Ae_k=exp(−c k^β)e_k on ℓ², with c,β>0, and use M_r={x:Σk^{2r}|x_k|²≤1}. Write L=log(1/δ).

For sufficiently large L define tδ=((L−(r/β)log L)/c)^{1/β} and Nδ=⌊tδ⌋. The subtraction is part of the parameter rule; Nδ is positive once δ is sufficiently small.

Sharp logarithmic order with a valid parameter rule

The cutoff error is O(L^(−r/β)) for the stated Nδ. This is also the deterministic minimax order on M_r. The leading equivalence Nδ∼(L/c)^{1/β} alone does not guarantee convergence for every sequence with that equivalence.

Derivation or proof

As before B(N)≤(N+1)^(−r), and now S(N)=exp(cN^β). Since Nδ≤tδ, δS(Nδ)≤exp(−L+L−(r/β)log L)=L^(−r/β). Because tδ∼(L/c)^{1/β}, the bias has the same order. Differentiating the analytic function at zero then givesBᵀ(Aᵀ)^kv=0 for allk≥0. Cayley–Hamilton reduces these equations tok=0,…,n−1. Search error can therefore be driven to zero by exhaustive finite enumeration or a matching lower bound, while model discrepancy remains logically independent. Revised question

Which state equivalence preserves every remaining decision, and in which direction does partition refinement move?

The source reports Bellman quotient sequences such as8→6→3→2→1. Counts alone do not show that a quotient is valid. A finite-horizon recursion gives an exact sufficient equivalence, identifies the needed state information and explains when partition counts can legitimately decrease.

Definitions and assumptions

At time t, a state s has a finite legal action set A_t(s), immediate costs c_t(s,a), deterministic successor T_t(s,a), and terminal cost h at time L. Infeasible continuations have cost+∞.

Define equivalence backward: terminal states are equivalent when h agrees; at time t, states are equivalent when they have identical action labels and, for each action, identical immediate cost and equivalent successors. Keep the minimum accumulated prefix cost for each class.

Continuation-preserving quotient theorem

Equivalent states have equal cost for every legal labeled continuation and equal Bellman value. Replacing them by their class and retaining the cheapest prefix preserves the global optimum. On one fixed state set, a refinement splits classes and cannot lower their number.

Derivation or proof

At the terminal stage, continuation cost is the agreed terminal value. Assuming the assertion at t+1, matching action labels, costs and successor classes gives matching cost for an action followed by any tail. Induction proves the full continuation statement and hence equality of its minimum. Two equivalent prefixes differ only in accumulated cost, so every future suffix adds the same amount; discarding the more expensive prefix cannot remove an optimum. For the partition direction, P refines Q precisely when every P-block lies within a Q-block; the induced map from P-blocks onto Q-blocks is surjective, so |P|≥|Q|. A decreasing numerical sequence may instead reflect backward horizons, elimination of unreachable states or deliberate validated merging; its direction is not evidence of a refinement theorem.

Worked example

At the final decision use states a,b,c with two actions L,R and cost vectors a=(0,10), b=(10,0), c=(0,10). All successors have zero terminal cost.

a and c are equivalent and can merge. State b also has minimum value zero but is not continuation-equivalent: restricting the future to actionL yields cost0 froma and10 fromb. Thus equal scalar Bellman values are insufficient for a quotient required to survive changes in the allowed continuation set.

The quotient has a constructive correctness invariant rather than only an attractive reduction count.

Any future factor sees the processed region only through the retained variables and resources. Keeping their cheaper prefix is valid by direct substitution, and induction over the processing order proves the recursion. The D^κ bound counts boundary assignments, not extra partitions or capacities. For repeated layers, concatenate an optimal prefix to each one-layer transition and minimize the intermediate boundary state; this is precisely min-plus multiplication. Definitions and assumptions

Let Π_k be all set partitions of a k-element boundary. Write p∨q for the least common coarsening and define M_pq=1 when p∨q has one block, zero otherwise, over F₂.

A cut is a two-coloring with vertex one fixed to colorzero; there are2^(k−1) cuts. Define C_p,c=1 when every block ofp is monochromatic under cutc. A weighted family assigns a finite costw(p) to each available partition.

M=CCᵀ over F₂ and rank M=2^(k−1). Processing available C-rows in nondecreasing cost and retaining only linearly independent rows yields at most2^(k−1) representatives, preserving min{w(p):p∨q is one block} for every completionq.

The one-block partition has C-row equal to the trivial-cut unit vector. Each nontrivial bipartition has row equal to that unit vector plus its own cut unit vector. These rows span all2^(k−1) cut columns, so C has full column rank. Consequently Cᵀ is onto and C is injective, giving rank(CCᵀ)=2^(k−1). For weighted preservation, a discarded row is an F₂-sum of retained rows of no greater weight. In general a minimal basis has the predictable-degree property: polynomial combinations have degree governed by the largest coefficient-degree plus corresponding minimal index. Counting allowed polynomial coefficients gives the nullity formula. The direct calculation above needs no canonical-form algorithm. Definitions and assumptions

Let A(t),E(t) be differentiable complex matrices, λ(t) a simple finite eigenvalue, Av=λEv and u* A=λu*E. Assumeu*Ev≠0. For λ=σ+iω≠0 defineζ=−σ/(σ²+ω²)^{1/2}.

Derivation or proof

DifferentiateAv=λEv: A′v+Av′=λ′Ev+λE′v+λEv′. Multiply byu*. The terms involvingv′ cancel becauseu*A=λu*E, leavingλ′u*Ev=u*(A′−λE′)v. The denominator assumption permits division and reveals the normalization sensitivity. Differentiatingζ=−σ(σ²+ω²)^{-1/2} and collecting terms gives the damping formula. Scaling either eigenvector cancels from the quotient, so no Euclidean normalization is required. At a multiple or defective eigenvalue a differentiable branch need not exist; atλ=0 the damping ratio itself is undefined. Revised question

Which state really advances by a fixed residue increment, and does its observed period equal the period of that full state?

The recovered experiment used the formula p=k/gcd(k,r) for a buffer-related residue. That formula has a complete elementary proof once the state and update are stated. It certifies an orbit of a cyclic permutation; it does not, by itself, certify the period of every hidden state in a processor or execution.

Definitions and assumptions

Fix integers k≥1 and r. The state space is Z/kZ, and the update is F(x)=x+r modk. Let d=gcd(k,r), taking a nonnegative gcd.

A period is a positive integer p with F^p(x)=x. The least such integer is the orbit length. An observation h can identify different states, so h(F^n(x)) may have a shorter period.

A rotating residue has an exact period and a complete orbit decomposition

Every orbit of F has length p=k/d. There are exactly d orbits, each consisting of the residues in one congruence class modulo d. In particular, a genuine period two requires k even and r congruent to k/2 modulo k.

Derivation or proof

Iteration gives F^n(x)=x+nr modk. Return to the initial state is equivalent to k dividing nr, independently of x. Write k=dk₀ and r=dr₀ with gcd(k₀,r₀)=1. Then k divides nr exactly when k₀ divides nr₀, which is equivalent to k₀ dividing n by coprimality. The least positive n is therefore k₀. Every increment is divisible by d, so an orbit remains in one class modulo d. That class has k/d elements, exactly the orbit length, proving equality and the d-orbit count. For length two, k/d=2 forces d=k/2 and hence r=(k/2) times an odd integer modulo k.

Worked example

Use the newly declared exact case k=12,r=8, then compare an observation that retains only parity.

Here d=4 and the orbit through zero is0→8→4→0. The remaining orbits are the other three congruence classes modulo four. The full residue has period three, but parity is constant along every one of these orbits, with observed period one. For a separate period-two case k=6,r=3, the orbit0→3→0 satisfies the theorem exactly. These integers illustrate the algebra; they are not asserted to be historical hardware parameters.

The period formula becomes an exact state-transition theorem, while the distinction between state period and observation period remains explicit.

Scope

The source bullet does not define the original k,r variables or all buffer and port components. A period in one counter cannot establish a full-state recurrence without proving that the update has this cyclic form and that the observation is sufficient.

Further development

For a product of cyclic counters, derive the joint period from the least common multiple of the individual orbit lengths, then characterize which observation maps collapse that joint period.

Revised question

Which hidden states share the same observation, and do their next observations agree well enough to define an autonomous reduced update?

The report that Pathfinder required port-side state points to a substantive mathematical issue: an observed counter need not be a sufficient state. A general quotient criterion and a finite example show exactly when state augmentation is necessary and when a short observation history recovers the missing variable.

Definitions and assumptions

Let F:X→X be deterministic dynamics and h:X→Y an observation. A closed reduced update is a map g:h(X)→h(X) satisfying h∘F=g∘h.

The fibers of h are the sets of states giving the same observation. The example below is explicitly new: X=F₂² with state(b,p), update F(b,p)=(b+p,p+1), and h(b,p)=b. All additions are modulo two.

A hidden port variable can prevent a deterministic observation from closing

A reduced map g exists exactly when h(x)=h(x′) implies h(Fx)=h(Fx′). In the two-bit example, the counter b alone does not close, but the ordered pair of consecutive observations(b_t,b_(t+1)) determines the full state uniquely.

Derivation or proof

Necessity follows by applying g to equal observations. For sufficiency, define g(y)=h(Fx) for any representative with h(x)=y; the fiber condition makes this independent of the representative. In the example, states(0,0) and(0,1) both show b=0, but their next b values are zero and one, violating the criterion. From the update, b_(t+1)=b_t+p_t, so p_t=b_t+b_(t+1). Thus two consecutive output bits reconstruct(b_t,p_t). This is an exact observability calculation rather than an appeal to an unspecified hidden-state effect.

The following are equivalent: kerO⊂kerG; G=LO for some L; and GᵀG≼λOᵀO for some finiteλ≥0. The optimal λ is the square of the smallest possible recovery norm.

Extend L by zero on the orthogonal complement of rangeO; finite dimensionality makes it bounded. Its norm gives the quadratic inequality. Conversely that inequality forces Gx=0 whenever Ox=0, recovering the kernel condition. Every factorization gives the inequality with λ=||L||², while the smallest possible norm on rangeO is exactly sup_(Ox≠0)||Gx||/||Ox||. This proves the optimal constant as well as existence.

Exact prime valuations remove that problem and also clarify a normalization subtlety: for squares, n=cw² describes all hits only when the coefficient c is squarefree, or when a restricted subfamily is intended.

Definitions and assumptions

Fix integers c≥1 and d≥2. Write c=∏p p^(e_p), and define a=∏_(p|c)p^(−e_p mod d), using residues in{0,…,d−1}.

Let A_(c,d)(N) count positive n≤N for which cn is an integer d-th power; it counts n once, regardless of the possible sign choices for its root.

The linear perfect-power branch has an exact valuation formula and never becomes finite through underflow

The hits are exactly n=at^d with t≥1. Therefore A_(c,d)(N)=floor((N/a)^(1/d)), interpreted by an exact integer d-th root. In particular this branch is infinite for every positive c. For d=2, a is the squarefree part of c.

Derivation or proof

For each prime p, the condition that cn be a d-th power is e_p+v_p(n)≡0 mod d, with e_p=0 for primes not dividing c. Thus v_p(n) is the prescribed least residue plus a nonnegative multiple of d. Collecting all prime powers gives n=at^d. Conversely ca has every valuation divisible by d, so cn=(u t)^d with integer u=(ca)^(1/d). The bijection t↦at^d proves the count and infinitude. No approximate coefficient or limiting classification is required.

Take c=12,d=2.

Here12=2²·3, so a=3 and ca=36. All hits are n=3t² with square root m=6t. Up to N=100 there are exactly five:3,12,27,48,75. Writing only n=12w² would omit3,27,75 and therefore requires an extra convention. For c=72 the squarefree part is two and the roots are m=12t. Huge c can delay the first hit beyond a finite search range but cannot make the infinite family bounded.

The classifier obtains an exact structural branch and a reproducible population count.

This theorem is for a positive linear coefficient with zero constant term. A general polynomial or shifted linear core needs additional congruence and integrality conditions. A finite prefix containing no hits is not a finiteness certificate.

The finite disjunction implies E by substituting each pair and checking its equality. Revised question

Which exact algebraic certificate can discharge an irreducibility task, and what additional theorem is needed before a curve classification follows?

The recovered October workload distinguishes curve modules, irreducible equations and point-carrying cases. These are different mathematical obligations. A reusable reduction certificate can settle a polynomial irreducibility statement, while point completeness still requires the actual arithmetic argument. The examples here are explicitly chosen models, not reconstructions of the unavailable positive-k equations.

Definitions and assumptions

A polynomial f in Z[x] is primitive when its coefficients have gcd one. Reduction modulo a prime p preserves its degree if p does not divide the leading coefficient.

Irreducibility is over a specified field. A rational-point completeness theorem asserts that every rational point satisfying the stated curve equation occurs in a specified list or parametrization.

A sound finite-field route and its scope

If a primitive f in Z[x] has degree-preserving irreducible reduction modulo p, then f is irreducible over Q. For degree two or three, irreducibility over F_p is equivalent to having no root in F_p. Neither statement supplies all rational points on an associated curve.

Derivation or proof

Gauss’s lemma turns a nontrivial rational factorization into f=gh with primitive integer factors of positive degree. Because the leading coefficient of f is nonzero modulo p, both leading coefficients of g and h are nonzero modulo p. Reduction therefore preserves their positive degrees and contradicts irreducibility of the reduction. For a quadratic or cubic over a field, any nontrivial factorization has a linear factor, equivalent to a root; conversely a root gives a linear divisor. In higher degree, rootlessness alone is insufficient because both factors may have degree at least two. This proves a precise certificate rule with no appeal to numeric root approximations. The logical separation from point classification is visible already in a hyperelliptic equation y²=f(x): irreducibility of f does not determine which rational x make f(x) a square.

Worked example

Use f=x³−x+1 and contrast a fourth-degree polynomial.

Modulo two, f becomes x³+x+1. Its values at 0 and 1 are both 1, so it is an irreducible cubic and f is irreducible over Q. The curve y²=x³−x+1 has the easily checked rational points (0,±1), (1,±1) and (3,±5). Irreducibility alone neither produces these points nor proves that any proposed finite list is complete. For a sharper algebraic caution, x⁴+1 factors modulo three as (x²+x+2)(x²+2x+2), although it is irreducible over Q: after x↦x+1 it becomes x⁴+4x³+6x²+4x+2, which is Eisenstein at two. A failed reduction test is therefore inconclusive.

One can replay small irreducibility certificates exactly while keeping the missing curve-completeness argument visible.

Scope

The historical compilation and class-list counts are retrieved claims, not independently replayed here. No equation, discriminant, shared sublemma or Lean theorem name absent from the receipt is invented. The displayed models establish certificate logic only.

Further development

Create a dependency graph whose nodes separate polynomial irreducibility, local solubility, descent bounds and final point completeness; attach explicit prime-reduction or Eisenstein witnesses to the first class and require a theorem connecting the remaining classes before marking a curve classified.

Which exact cubic identities can be checked directly, and what is still required to prove the claimed global uniqueness of a norm-equation solution?

The retrieved monograph claims a complete solution of u³+4v³=107 and records two units. The available evidence does not include its slab bounds or unit-exponent exclusion certificate. We can nevertheless derive the exact norm form, replay the units and the displayed solution, and state the missing completeness obligation without substituting a finite search for it.

Definitions and assumptions

Let z³=−4 and use the integral basis 1,z,z² of the order Z[z]. Define N(a+bz+cz²) as the determinant of multiplication on this free Z-module.

An element with norm ±1 is a unit of this order because its integer multiplication matrix has an integer inverse.

Exact cubic norm and unit identities

N(a+bz+cz²)=a³−4b³+16c³+12abc. The elements η=5−3z+2z² and ε=1−z−z² both have norm one. Also N(u−vz)=u³+4v³, and (u,v)=(−1,3) gives norm 107.

Derivation or proof

Multiplication by a+bz+cz² in the indicated basis has matrix [[a,−4c,−4b],[b,a,−4c],[c,b,a]]. Expanding its determinant gives the stated cubic form, proving the identity without numeric algebraic approximations. For η, the four contributions are 125,108,128,−360, summing to one. For ε they are 1,4,−16,12, again summing to one. Determinants multiply, so multiplication by any ηʳεˢ preserves a norm equation. Setting (a,b,c)=(u,−v,0) gives u³+4v³; the displayed point gives −1+108=107. These calculations prove valid transport in a three-coordinate norm surface. They do not show that unit multiplication keeps c=0, nor that all norm-107 elements lie in an asserted seed orbit. A binary equation is an intersection of the norm surface with the plane c=0, so returning to that plane is an additional exact condition.

Worked example

Compute one unit action on the displayed norm element.

The element −1−3z corresponds to (−1,−3,0). Multiplication by ε=(1,−1,−1) gives (−13,−2,4), using z³=−4. Its norm remains 107 by multiplicativity, but its z² coefficient is four, so it is no longer a solution of the original two-variable equation.

The unit identities are verified, while the binary-plane return problem remains explicit.

The historical statement that (−1,3) is the only integer solution is not independently established here. A 3,631-candidate slab or modular period is not a global bound unless its reduction theorem and all excluded exponent classes are supplied and replayed.

Revised question

How can linear Diophantine lifting and prime-exponent constraints yield a complete, exactly countable population?

The retrieved examples illustrate two forms of integer lifting: an affine line of solutions and a finite product of exponent lattices. Both require divisibility conditions, rather than a real-valued inverse followed by rounding. The exponent formulation is also the correct setting for Smith normal form compatibility tests.

Definitions and assumptions

A positive integer has a unique vector of nonnegative prime exponents.

A unimodular integer change of variables has determinant ±1 and preserves the integer lattice; Smith normal form diagonalizes an integer linear map using such changes.

Complete affine and multiplicative solution sets

All integer solutions of 2x+3y=1 are (x,y)=(−1+3t,1−2t), t∈Z. The equation x²y³=2²⁰3¹² has exactly twelve positive integer solutions, indexed by 0≤r≤3 and 0≤s≤2 as x=2^(10−3r)3^(6−3s), y=2^(2r)3^(2s).

Derivation or proof

Reducing 2x+3y=1 modulo three gives x≡−1 mod 3, so x=−1+3t; substitution forces y=1−2t. Every t works, proving completeness and injectivity. For the multiplicative equation, no prime other than two or three can divide x or y, because all exponents are nonnegative. Write x=2ᵃ3ᶜ and y=2ᵇ3ᵈ. Unique factorization gives 2a+3b=20 and 2c+3d=12. The first equation forces b even, b=2r, and then a=10−3r≥0, so r=0,1,2,3. The second similarly gives d=2s and c=6−3s≥0, so s=0,1,2. These choices are independent and unique, producing 4·3=12 solutions. More generally, if UAV=diag(d₁,…,d_r,0,…) is a Smith decomposition of an exponent map, integer solvability requires d_i to divide (Ub)_i and zero coordinates of Ub to vanish; nonnegativity is an additional constraint after applying V.

Worked example

Enumerate two endpoints and construct a reversible address.

At (r,s)=(0,0), (x,y)=(2¹⁰3⁶,1); at (3,2), (x,y)=(2,2⁶3⁴). The address j=3r+s runs from zero to eleven; division with remainder recovers r=⌊j/3⌋ and s=j mod 3. Thus the count and inverse lookup are both exact.

Prime-exponent reduction proves every listed point and excludes every omitted positive point.

Scope

Negative or zero solutions need separate sign and support cases. Smith invariant factors alone do not enforce nonnegativity, and a claimed perfect-cube compatibility obstruction requires the actual lattice map, not just a numerical determinant.

Further development

Combine Smith coordinates with polyhedral lattice-point enumeration to count bounded exponent populations and optimize a stated linear cost in the original exponents, preserving a certificate of every divisibility and sign condition.
