Revised question

Which exact incidence factorization explains invertibility, determinant and solution of a GCD linear system?

The recovered GCD-kernel discussion has a precise arithmetic factorization. A related cumulative-sum kernel explains why a dense covariance matrix can have an integer tridiagonal inverse. These are separate examples of a common incidence-matrix principle.

Definitions and assumptions

Let G_n have entries gcd(i,j), 1≤i,j≤n, and E_ij=1 when j divides i, zero otherwise. Let φ be Euler’s totient.

For the second example, let L_ij=1 when j≤i and K_ij=min(i,j).

Exact arithmetic and chain-incidence factorizations

G_n=E diag(φ(1),…,φ(n))Eᵀ, so det G_n=∏_(j=1)^nφ(j)>0. Also K=LLᵀ and K⁻¹=DᵀD, where D has diagonal one and subdiagonal −1. Its diagonal is (2,…,2,1) and its adjacent off-diagonals are −1.

Derivation or proof

The divisor identity Σ_(d|m)φ(d)=m follows by grouping the integers 1,…,m according to their gcd with m. Hence (E diagφ Eᵀ)_ij=Σ_(d|i,d|j)φ(d)=gcd(i,j). E is lower triangular with diagonal one, proving the determinant and positive definiteness. Solving Gx=b reduces to two triangular substitutions and positive scalar divisions; the inverse incidence matrix is the divisibility Möbius matrix, by the identity Σ_(d|m)μ(d)=0 for m>1. For the chain kernel, (LLᵀ)_ij counts indices at most both i and j, giving min(i,j). D=L⁻¹ because first differences invert cumulative sums. Therefore K⁻¹=DᵀD; direct multiplication gives the stated tridiagonal entries. The last diagonal is one because the final coordinate occurs in only the last row of D.

Worked example

Check the n=3 chain kernel and a GCD determinant.

K=[[1,1,1],[1,2,2],[1,2,3]] has inverse [[2,−1,0],[−1,2,−1],[0,−1,1]]. The GCD matrix [[1,1,1],[1,2,1],[1,1,3]] has determinant φ(1)φ(2)φ(3)=2. Both identities are verified by exact matrix multiplication.

Dense kernels can have sparse inverses because they encode an integrated local difference operator.

Scope

The min kernel is a newly chosen chain model, not an identification of every unspecified normalized GCD kernel in the source. A factorization over Q does not imply its inverse has integer entries; the totient diagonal generally introduces denominators.

Further development

Replace gcd(i,j) by f(gcd(i,j)); Möbius inversion gives diagonal weights (f*μ)(d). Positivity of those weights is then an explicit sufficient condition for positive definiteness on the initial divisor-closed set.

The ramification index is d, contributing d−1 at each of the m finite branch points. At infinity the equation has orders d·ord(y)=m·ord(x); dividing by δ shows that there are δ points above infinity, each with ramification index d/δ. Their total contribution is d−δ. How can a denominator be inverted exactly on the valid components of a polynomial quotient without losing its exceptional components?

The recovered gcd branch splitting has a clean Chinese-remainder proof. It turns an informal instruction to avoid zero denominators into an exact decomposition of a finite algebra. The squarefree hypothesis is the structural reason the branches separate.

Definitions and assumptions

Let K be a field, p∈K[t] squarefree, and a∈K[t]. Set g=gcd(p,a), h=p/g, with monic choices.

Write R=K[t]/(p). A component is regular for a when multiplication by a is invertible on it.

Exact regular/exceptional decomposition

g and h are coprime, and R≅K[t]/(g)×K[t]/(h). The image of a is zero in the first factor and invertible in the second; a Bézout identity supplies its inverse there.

Derivation or proof

Because p is squarefree, no irreducible factor dividing g can also divide h. The Chinese remainder map therefore has inverse constructed from Bézout polynomials ug+vh=1, proving the algebra isomorphism. Every factor of g divides a, so a is zero modulo g. Conversely, any common divisor of a and h would divide p and a, hence g, contradicting coprimality of g and h. Thus gcd(a,h)=1, and extended Euclid gives ra+sh=1; r is an exact inverse of a modulo h. No root approximations or heuristic branch labels enter. When g=1 there is no exceptional component; when h=1 every component is exceptional. These cases are naturally interpreted using the zero quotient factor.

Worked example

Take K=Q, p=(t−1)(t+1)(t−2) and a=t−1.

Here g=t−1 and h=t²−t−2. In K[t]/(h), (t−1)(t/2)=(t²−t)/2=1, so t/2 is the regular inverse. In the factor t=1, a is zero. Hence an expression b/a can be evaluated using bt/2 only on the h component; the t=1 component still requires its original undivided equation. For contrast, if p=(t−1)², then g=t−1 and h=t−1 are not coprime: the quotient contains a nonzero nilpotent and cannot be replaced by a product of two point factors.

The decomposition makes every denominator decision and exceptional branch auditable.

How do local completion counts yield a global bijection between feasible objects and integer addresses?

The recovered query-space work emphasizes exact addresses, inverse lookup, pagination and uniform sampling. These are consequences of a single prefix-partition theorem. It is the disjoint completion population, not the apparent size of an ambient search box, that determines valid addresses.

Definitions and assumptions

Let Ω⊆{0,1}ⁿ be a finite nonempty population ordered lexicographically with 0 before 1. For a prefix q, let C(q) count its feasible completions.

The empty prefix has C(∅)=|Ω| and C(q)=C(q0)+C(q1); a feasible complete word has count one.

Rank/unrank bijection and unbiased sampling

There is an exact bijection rank:Ω→{0,…,|Ω|−1}. At prefix q, all q0 completions occupy the first C(q0) addresses; the q1 block occupies the following C(q1). A uniform address therefore gives a uniform object.

Derivation or proof

At a node q, split its contiguous address interval into disjoint initial and final blocks with those lengths. For unranking, compare the residual address r with C(q0): choose 0 when r<C(q0), otherwise choose 1 and replace r by r−C(q0). The chosen block has positive length and its residual address is valid; induction reaches exactly one feasible leaf. For ranking, scan a feasible word and add C(q0) whenever its next bit is 1. At each step these operations are inverse translations on the two disjoint blocks, proving the global bijection. Consequently P(unrank(R)=ω)=1/|Ω| when R is uniform. Conditional populations use the same construction below a fixed prefix. To draw an exact uniform integer from random bits, rejection sampling of a b-bit integer with 2ᵇ≥|Ω| is unbiased; reducing that integer modulo |Ω| is generally biased unless the modulus divides 2ᵇ.

The list is 000,001,010,100,110 with ranks 0,…,4; the prefix 1 has two completions. To sample one of five objects, generate three fair bits and reject addresses 5,6,7. Each valid address has conditional probability 1/5. Direct reduction of all eight bit strings modulo five instead gives probabilities (2,2,2,1,1)/8 and is not uniform.

The population has a reversible exact index and a precisely stated sampling distribution.

A deterministic seed supplies reproducibility, not by itself a proof of uniformity or cryptographic unpredictability. If distinct source objects were merged, the address bijection would index the quotient rather than the original population.

Which requested outputs are identifiable from a given observation, even when the entire hidden state is not?

The recovered kernel criterion is a complete finite-dimensional identifiability theorem. It separates state reconstruction from recovering a particular target. The distinction prevents unnecessary sensing and makes a missing-information claim testable by an explicit nullspace vector.

Definitions and assumptions

Let V,W,Z be finite-dimensional vector spaces over Q or R, with observation H:V→W and target G:V→Z.

The target is identifiable when Hx=Hy implies Gx=Gy for every x,y∈V.

Kernel factorization criterion

The following are equivalent: the target is identifiable; ker H⊆ker G; and there is a linear L:W→Z such that G=LH. L is uniquely determined on im H but need not be unique on all W.

Derivation or proof

If the target is identifiable, set y=0 and x∈ker H to obtain Gx=0. Conversely, Hx=Hy means x−y∈ker H, so kernel inclusion gives Gx=Gy. To construct L on im H, define L(Hx)=Gx. If Hx=Hy the kernel condition makes this independent of the representative, and linearity follows from the linearity of H and G. Extend a basis of im H to a basis of W and define L arbitrarily on the complement. Then G=LH. The converse factorization immediately implies kernel inclusion. A violating vector v with Hv=0 but Gv≠0 is therefore a complete impossibility certificate: x and x+v have identical data and different targets.

Observe Hx=(x₁+x₂,x₂+x₃) and ask for Gx=x₁+2x₂+x₃.

Here ker H is span((1,−1,1)), and G annihilates this vector. The reconstruction is Gx=(1,1)Hx. Asking instead for x₁ fails, since its value changes along the kernel. In four dimensions, observing only the first two coordinates leaves a two-dimensional fibre; two further independent scalar linear measurements are necessary and sufficient to reconstruct the whole state, although fewer may suffice for a particular G.

The theorem identifies precisely which uncertainty matters for a requested mathematical output.

Scope

Nonlinear, noisy or restricted-state observations require revised conditions. Dimension counting is a lower bound for full linear reconstruction, not a universal lower bound for arbitrary discontinuous encodings or finite-state problems.

This is a worst-case conditioning theorem; a particular floating-point algorithm can add further rounding errors, while correlated input errors may cancel and require a joint model. Every solution satisfies y′=T(t)y if and only if B′(t)+B(t)A(t)=T(t)B(t) for every t. For full-row-rank B, some T exists at a given time exactly when ker B⊆ker(B′+BA).

Revised question

What is the minimum guaranteed measurement cost for determining a target on a finite uncertainty set?

The recovered decision recurrence becomes rigorous once terminal conditions, deterministic outcomes and admissible progress are specified. Its proof is an exact decision-tree induction. This gives a constructive optimum rather than an assertion that one greedy panel is best.

Definitions and assumptions

Let S be a finite set of possible states and g:S→D the target decision. An experiment e has positive cost c_e and partitions S into outcome fibres S_(e,y).

A terminal set is one on which g is constant. Ignore experiments whose only nonempty outcome is S itself; they cannot improve a worst-case exact decision.

Bellman minimax recursion

If the available tests separate every pair with different target values, V(S)=0 on terminal sets and otherwise V(S)=min_e[c_e+max_(y:S_(e,y)≠∅)V(S_(e,y))], restricting to experiments with all nonempty fibres proper subsets. This equals the minimum worst-case cost of an exact adaptive decision tree.

Derivation or proof

A decision tree must choose some experiment e first. An adversarial outcome can choose the most expensive remaining fibre, so its worst-case cost is at least c_e+max_y V(S_(e,y)). Minimizing over the first choice gives a lower bound on every tree. Conversely, choose an experiment attaining the finite minimum and attach optimal subtrees on its proper fibres. Induction on |S| constructs a tree achieving exactly that cost. Pairwise separability ensures a nonterminal set has a useful splitting test and a finite exact tree; positive costs make a non-splitting first experiment wasteful. This proves both existence and optimality. For noisy observations the fibres would be replaced by feasible posterior sets and terminal robustness would need a separate definition.

Worked example

Identify one of three states a,b,c.

Experiment e₁ costs one and partitions {a} from {b,c}; e₂ costs two and partitions {b} from {a,c}; a direct three-way experiment costs four. Performing e₁ first and, only if necessary, e₂ has worst-case cost three. Every one-test cheaper choice leaves a two-state ambiguity requiring the other test, so the Bellman optimum is three. The early a outcome costs only one, showing the adaptive branch structure.

The decision policy and its lower bound arise from the same exact recurrence.

Scope

A worst-case optimum need not minimize expected cost under a prior. Historical panel speedups or prediction accuracies cannot be inferred from this finite theorem without the original states, tests and evaluation data.

Revised question

Can the recovered phase integral be proved, including its logarithmic singularities and rational coefficient?

The exact phase set makes this one of the strongest independently checkable October identities. Fourier analysis reduces the integral to a finite Bernoulli-polynomial sum. Logarithmic endpoint and interior singularities are square-integrable and are part of the proof, not exclusions from it.

Definitions and assumptions

Let S={0,1,2,4,11}, θ_s=2πs/17 and P(x)=∏_(s∈S)(2x−2cos θ_s).

Define I=∫_(−1)^1 log²|P(x)|/√(1−x²)dx, equivalently ∫₀^πlog²|P(cos t)|dt. Let B₂(u)=u²−u+1/6 and {u} denote fractional part.

Exact five-phase integral

I=(955/867)π³. More generally I/π³=Σ_(s,r∈S)[B₂({(s−r)/17})+B₂({(s+r)/17})] for this convention of product factors.

Derivation or proof

The factorization 2cos t−2cos θ=e^(−it)(e^(it)−e^(iθ))(e^(it)−e^(−iθ)) shows that log|2cos t−2cos θ|=−2Σ_(n≥1)cos(nt)cos(nθ)/n in L²(0,π). One can justify the boundary Fourier series by radial regularization of log|1−re^(iu)| and L² convergence of its square-summable coefficients as r↑1. Local logarithmic singularities, including the doubled endpoint singularity when θ=0, are L², so the factorization agrees with this limit. Summing over S gives −2Σa_ncos(nt)/n, where a_n=Σ_scos(nθ_s). Parseval yields I=2πΣa_n²/n². The identity2cos u cos v=cos(u−v)+cos(u+v), followed by Σ_(n≥1)cos(2πnu)/n²=π²B₂({u}), gives the finite formula. Evaluating its fifty rational B₂ terms with denominator17² gives exactly955/867. Individual B₂ terms may be negative, but the full quadratic expression is nonnegative for every phase multiset by its Parseval representation. This also checks the factor of two and shows why estimating each pair contribution independently can obscure the positivity of the original integral.

Worked example

Give a rational-only arithmetic certificate for the coefficient.

For residues k modulo17, B₂(k/17)=k²/289−k/17+1/6. The verifier loops over all25 ordered pairs (s,r), adds the difference and sum residues, and obtains Fraction(955,867). Root’s independent audit computes the same finite sum separately.

The integral is established analytically, and its final rational coefficient is independently replayable without numerical quadrature.

Scope

A different normalization of each product factor would add constants inside the logarithm and change the integral. No KZ or group-closure conclusion follows merely from this phase integral.

Further development

For any finite rational phase set, derive the corresponding Bernoulli sum and classify sets with equal quadratic logarithmic energy; add higher moments only after proving convergence and the required multiple Fourier convolution identities.

Which consequences of the recovered braid and determinant relations can be proved without the missing KZ matrices?

Definitions and assumptions

Let ζ=exp(2πi/17). Assume unitary5×5 matrices R₁,R₂ satisfy the braid relation, det R_i=ζ⁹ and (R₁R₂)³=ζ⁴I.

Set T_i=ζ⁵R_i and G={g∈U(5):det(g)¹⁷=1}. The hypothesis that a generated subgroup is dense is separate from these finite relations.

Exact twist and split determinant group

T_i∈SU(5), they satisfy the braid relation, and (T₁T₂)³=I. If additionally T_i³⁴=I, they define a quotient of Δ(2,3,34). Moreover G≅SU(5)×μ₁₇ as compact groups, via (S,ξ)↦ξS.

Derivation or proof

Twisting a5×5 matrix by ζ⁵ multiplies its determinant by ζ²⁵; thus det T_i=ζ³⁴=1. Both sides of the braid relation gain the same scalar ζ¹⁵. The central relation gains ζ³⁰, cancelling ζ⁴ because ζ³⁴=1. Put a=T₁T₂T₁ and b=T₁T₂. The braid relation gives a²=b³=I, and b⁻¹a=T₁, so the extra relation T₁³⁴=I gives the triangle presentation with orders dividing2,3,34. For the group decomposition, ξ∈μ₁₇ has determinant ξ⁵. Since5 is invertible modulo17, this scalar determinant map is an automorphism; its inverse exponent is7. Given g∈G, set ξ=det(g)⁷ and S=ξ⁻¹g. Then det S=det(g)^(1−35)=1. This is a continuous inverse to (S,ξ)↦ξS, and the intersection SU(5)∩μ₁₇I is trivial, proving the product isomorphism.

The determinant of (R₁R₂)³ is ζ⁵⁴=ζ³, while det(ζ⁴I)=ζ²⁰=ζ³, so the reported relations are mutually compatible at determinant level. The twist makes both determinants and the central cube exactly one.

The arithmetic structure of the proposed compact closure is verified conditionally, with its missing density step explicit.

Finite order, irreducibility or a finite list of nonzero projector blocks does not alone prove density in SU(5). The actual matrices, unitarizing form and exclusion of finite and proper closed subgroups are not recovered; no claimed holonomy residual or Lean certificate is replayed.

Source receipt: root_coverage_5.json record 0. Original user question: not recovered verbatim

Revised question

How can a decision be certified when separate interval bounds overlap but the competing scores share the same uncertainty?

The recovered final October target is to certify a decision using common uncertainty and the cheapest sufficient measurement. Joint modeling preserves cancellation that is destroyed by independent interval bounds. The following theorem is deterministic and concerns abstract scores, with no empirical or financial forecast assumed.

Definitions and assumptions

Let X be a nonempty uncertainty set and let J_A,J_B:X→R be two scores, with larger preferred. Set δ(x)=J_A(x)−J_B(x).

A strict robust certificate is a positive lower bound m≤inf_(x∈X)δ(x). Attainment of the infimum is unnecessary if a bound is proved directly.

Joint dominance and measurement certificates

If inf_X(J_A−J_B)>0, A wins for every compatible state. In the shared model J_A=c+δ, J_B=c with δ∈[7/4,9/4], the margin is at least 7/4 regardless of the range of c. Separate interval subtraction can fail to certify the same fact.

Derivation or proof

The first assertion is immediate from the defining inequality for every x. Its content is the order of operations: subtraction must take place at the same uncertainty state before minimization. In general inf(A−B)≥inf A−sup B, but the inequality can be strict because the separate extrema need not occur at compatible states. For c∈[0,100], separate score ranges are A∈[7/4,409/4] and B∈[0,100]; their interval difference includes −393/4, even though the exact shared difference is always positive. A new measurement with result z and error bound ε restricts X to X_z={x:|h(x)−z|≤ε}; computing the margin on X_z can only improve its lower bound because X_z⊆X. A decision-sufficient experiment is one whose every nonempty outcome fibre gives a positive margin for one of the two directions.

Worked example

Suppose δ itself is measured with absolute error at most 1/10.

A result z=1/4 implies δ≥z−1/10=3/20>0, certifying A. A result z=1/20 gives δ∈[−1/20,3/20], so it does not certify either direction. With several possible tests, their costs and outcome fibres can be inserted into the finite Bellman recurrence to identify the cheapest guaranteed decision procedure.

The certificate exploits correlation exactly and states which remaining uncertainty matters.

Scope

Overlapping separate intervals do not imply an undecidable joint model, while a positive estimate without an error bound is not a robust certificate. This theorem supplies no calibration of an empirical uncertainty set.

Further development

Use polynomial or rational score models on a semialgebraic X and produce an exact positivity certificate for J_A−J_B; then optimize measurement cost subject to such certificates on every admissible outcome fibre.

Can the reported raw-state uniqueness be proved for every state with a small, independently checkable exact certificate?

The explicit recurrence allows a global theorem stronger than a collection of decoding tests. Equality of output words becomes a short-vector problem in an integer lattice. Exact dual bounds exclude every nonzero collision at once. The supplied certificate covers all 126 choices of five positions within nine steps; no enumeration of2^107 states and no trust in an LLL implementation is required.

Definitions and assumptions

Let M=2^107−1, A=3^121 moduloM, and b=2^26. States are integers0≤x_i<M with x_{i+1}=Ax_i moduloM; the raw observation is y_i=x_i modulo b. Since M≡1 modulo3, A is invertible moduloM.

For positions0≤p_0<⋯<p_4≤8 put g_j=p_j−p_0 and Λ_p={d∈Z^5:d_j≡A^{g_j}d_0 moduloM forj=1,…,4}. Let D=⌊(M−1)/b⌋=2^81−1.

Exact raw-state observability

For every five-position subset of{0,…,8}, the selected raw words uniquely determine the initial state. Four raw words cannot determine every state. Every supplied integer basis B_p has rows inΛ_p, |det B_p|=M^4, and DΣ_i|(B_p^(−1))_{ij}|<3/8 for each columnj.

Derivation or proof

The homomorphism Z^5→(Z/MZ)^4 sending d to(d_j−A^{g_j}d_0)_{j=1}^4 is onto: vary the final four coordinates while keeping d_0=0. Its kernelΛ_p therefore has indexM^4. The checker verifies lattice membership of every basis row and determinant magnitudeM^4, proving that its row lattice equalsΛ_p rather than merely a sublattice. It computes the inverse over rational numbers, verifies B_pB_p^(−1)=I, and checks the strict column bounds for all 126 position subsets. These properties alone suffice; the LLL routine used to find the bases is not trusted.

Suppose two states have the same five observed words. At each selected step their state difference is b d_j for an integerd_j with |d_j|≤D. The recurrence implies d_j≡A^{g_j}d_0 moduloM because b is invertible moduloM. Hence d=cB_p for some integer rowc. Each coordinate satisfies |c_j|=|(dB_p^(−1))_j|≤DΣ_i|(B_p^(−1))_{ij}|<3/8<1. Thusc=0, all selected state differences vanish, and invertibility of A takes equality atp_0 back to equality of the initial states. Four words range over at mostb^4=2^104 possibilities, whereas even the nonzero state set has M−1>2^104 elements. Pigeonhole therefore proves four-word impossibility.

The same dual bounds yield a decoder. Write selected states as y_j+bz_j with0≤z_j≤D. Their congruences define an affine lattice v+Λ_p, using v_0=0 and v_j=b^(−1)(A^{g_j}y_0−y_j) moduloM. For z=v+cB_p, each integerc_j lies in the exact interval obtained by applying the corresponding inverse column to the box0≤z≤D. Its width is below3/8, so it contains at most one integer. Round the interval endpoints exactly, reconstruct z and check all state bounds and observations; then reverse A^{p_0}. This is an actual exact decoder, not only an existence result.

Use each of the five states0,1,1234567890123456789,⌊M/3⌋ and M−1, and every five-position subset of the first nine raw outputs.

The largest dual bound is checked as an exact rational number strictly below3/8; its floating display, about0.368314147, is only for reading.

The universal conclusion comes from the determinant and dual-bound proof. The 630 fixtures separately verify the decoder implementation on concrete inputs.

Raw observations are consecutive generator steps at known positions, with the source recurrence and output convention stated above. Rejected/accepted-output sequences have hidden step counts and require a different theorem. This certificate makes no claim about their six-output threshold.

Revised question

What error correction follows from the all-state observation theorem, and are the observation counts information-theoretically necessary?

The finite-state trajectories define a code over the alphabet of26-bit words. The five-observation theorem controls its minimum Hamming distance without requiring linearity over a field. A puncturing argument then proves that the seven- and nine-word correction lengths cannot be improved for this full state population.

Definitions and assumptions

For5≤n≤9 let C_n={c_n(x):0≤x<M}, where c_n(x)=(y_0,…,y_{n−1}) is the raw trajectory. Hamming distance counts differing words, regardless of the bit distance within a corrupted word.

An arbitrary word corruption replaces one entire26-bit symbol. Unique correction oftcorruptions requires minimum code distance at least2t+1. Erasures at known positions are a different, easier observation model.

Exact distance and length-optimal correction

For5≤n≤9 the minimum distance of C_n is exactlyn−4. Thus seven raw outputs correct one arbitrary word error, and nine correct two. No code representing all M states over this alphabet can correct one error with six words or two errors with eight words.

Derivation or proof

If two distinct state codewords agreed at five positions in any n≤9, the preceding theorem would make the states equal. They therefore agree in at most four positions, giving distance at leastn−4. Conversely, for any code of minimum distanced, puncturing d−1fixed positions leaves an injective map: otherwise two original words differed only in those positions, contradicting the distance. Hence its population is at mostb^{n−d+1}. Since M>b^4, one has n−d+1≥5, or d≤n−4. This proves equality.

Two Hamming balls of radius t are disjoint when the minimum distance exceeds2t, by the triangle inequality; hence the stated seven- and nine-word codes uniquely correct the stated errors. An explicit decoder enumerates five-position subsets, applies the certified affine-lattice decoder, re-encodes each candidate and retains a state within the permitted Hamming radius. Enough clean positions remain to produce the true candidate, and the distance proof rules out a second one. Finally any code correcting t arbitrary errors has distance at least2t+1. Puncturing2t positions must be injective, giving M≤b^{n−2t}; sinceM>b^4, necessarily n≥5+2t. This proves the requested length lower bounds without a linear-code assumption.

Worked example

Start at x=1234567890123456789. In its first seven raw words replace position2 by that word plus12345 modulo b. In its first nine words instead corrupt positions1 and7 by offsets54321 and98765 modulo b.

The exact subset decoder returns the original state in both cases. The verification report retains all original and corrupted words. A word can be altered in many bits and still counts as one corruption in this model.

The finite decoder tests instantiate a globally proved distance theorem, and the puncturing bound proves that shorter full-population codes cannot have the same correction guarantee.

Scope

This is a coding theorem for the stated deterministic raw trajectories. It does not assert cryptographic unpredictability, statistical randomness or a correction guarantee when output positions are hidden by rejection sampling.

Further development

Study mixed errors and erasures: the same distance gives correction whenever2t+e<n−4. Implement a decoder that uses known erasure locations first, then prove exact failure/refusal conditions for inconsistent observations.
